newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: YEAREND-Modest '97 growth in Singapore electronics.
newsitem.headline: YEAREND-Modest '97 growth in Singapore electronics.

text.p: Singapore's key electronic sector is expected to grow modestly by slightly over 10 percent in 1997, down from its heyday of more than 20 percent in 1995 and 1994, analysts say
This is a small improvement over an estimated slow 10 percent growth in terms of value of output in 1996.
The second half of 1996 saw the sector hammered by plunging worldwide semiconductor prices, excess inventories and a slowdown in personal computer demand.

"Around 12 percent growth (in 1997) with most of the growth coming from the second half. 1997 will be the reverse of what happened in 1996. (The) first half next year will not be spectacular," said David Toh, analyst at ING Baring Securities.
Electronics output fell 1.7 percent in the third quarter of 1996, the first negative growth since 1992. It grew 23 percent and 12 percent in the first and second quarter respectively.
Toh said Singapore's electronics, which account for about half of the value of the manufacturing industry, could rise to a more exciting growth rate of "at least 15 percent" in 1998.

The sector is mainly tied to global demand for personal computers (PC), which is seen growing 15 percent in volume terms in 1997, analysts said. This is similar to 1996 and soft compared to the 23 percent rise in 1995.

Analysts said the outlook for the first half of 1997 was cautious -- depending on whether inventories move quickly enough after the seasonal pickup in demand during the Christmas period for PC-related products and components.
Growth hinges on two key divisions of Singapore's electronics -- data storage like hard disk drives and disk media, and semiconductors, which together make up a quarter of manufacturing output.
The hard disk drive division is expected to perform better than semiconductors in 1997 in terms of growth in value of sales, analysts said.
"There are fewer players, there is less competition, there is less excess inventories," said Toh.
The five major global players in hard disk drives are Seagate-Conner, Quantum, IBM, Western Digital, and Maxtor.

"The disk drive industry is still expected to ship 1.5 drives for every PC shipped this year. We would expect the disk drive industry in terms of units shipped to grow in the mid-teens region in 1997," said Patrick Yau, analyst at Schroders Securities.
Additional output expected from the relatively young disk media industry in Singapore is expected to help lift the sector, said Timothy Wong, research manager at Vickers Ballas.
But there is still concern over semiconductor prices, namely Dynamic Random Access Memories (DRAMs) and other memory chips.
"The overcapacity in the semiconductor industry can only be soaked up if the PC industry grows in excess of 30 percent in the coming two years, which we do not expect.
"Until then, prices will remain weak and Singapore wafer fabs, being price takers, will have to accept lower prices," said Yau.
The slowdown in the electronics industry in 1996 had caused at least two fabrication plants in Singapore to cut production, analysts said.
